title: Recurring calendar events: change one date or the series safely
description: Check ownership and edit scope before changing a recurring calendar event. Handle one-off changes, future schedules and exceptions without deleting the series.
lede: Before changing a repeating appointment, decide exactly which dates should change. Then verify that the editor offers that scope. This guide is published by Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars.
commonBelief: Every calendar editor asks whether a change applies to one occurrence or the whole series.

sections.heading: Describe the change before opening the editor
body: “Move next Tuesday’s lesson by one hour” is a one-occurrence change. “Starting next month, lessons are on Thursdays” changes a future schedule. “Correct the room for every meeting” may have a broader scope. These are different requests even when they start from the same event details screen.

Note the selected occurrence’s date and the surrounding dates that should remain unchanged. A short before-and-after list makes it easier to check the saved result. Do not use a real series to discover what an unfamiliar Save button does.

sections.heading: Check the calendar and your authority to edit
body: Find the calendar that owns the event and whether you are the organizer, an editor or a guest. Seeing a shared series does not by itself grant permission to change its schedule. Google documents guest modification as a permission the organizer can grant; viewing an invitation and managing it are different capabilities.

The Cloud Calendars source checks write access for the destination calendar. Its local calendars exclude reader access from editing, and system-calendar saves check whether content modifications are allowed. These checks do not prove that an attendee can update every organizer-owned meeting. If you cannot make the intended change, ask the organizer rather than creating a competing invitation.

sections.heading: Do not assume Cloud Calendars offers a scope prompt
body: The native editor source reviewed for this guide includes repeat patterns and an end-repeat setting. Its system-calendar save path selects future occurrences when an existing event has a recurrence rule at save time. It does not establish an interactive “only this occurrence” choice in that path. The local-calendar path saves a local event record and its rule; that is not evidence of equivalent per-occurrence editing.

For a one-date exception, or any change where the scope is unclear, stop before saving. Open the original event in its owning provider’s supported editor and use an explicitly offered scope. The code review is not a runtime test of your installed version, provider or series.

sections.heading: Use a supported scope, then check representative dates
body: Google Calendar’s computer instructions say to edit the recurring event, save and choose which events in the series receive the update. Read the actual choices shown for that event rather than assuming every provider uses identical labels or supports identical changes.

Apple’s Mac Calendar guide separately documents repeat frequency, custom patterns and when repetition stops. Those are Apple Calendar controls. Whichever supported editor you use, inspect the changed date, an earlier date that should remain unchanged and the next ordinary occurrence. For an invitation, also check the organizer’s saved event rather than treating a personal display change as confirmation that everyone’s meeting moved.

sections.heading: Preserve exceptions and choose end dates deliberately
body: A moved appointment or a skipped week is a reason to inspect an existing series before changing its rule. Record important exceptions first and check them afterward. It is not accurate to promise that every series edit preserves exceptions, or to claim that every edit automatically erases them: the result depends on the operation and provider.

Use a known final date for a course or temporary rota when that matches the real schedule. An ongoing birthday or continuing meeting may reasonably have no planned end. Do not force an arbitrary cutoff onto every repeat, and do not delete and recreate a series merely because it contains several exceptions.

sections.heading: If the result is unexpected, preserve the evidence
body: Compare the owning provider with Cloud Calendars on the exact affected date. Check the calendar name, selected occurrence, repeat pattern and any end condition you can inspect. Similar titles or a separately copied appointment can look like a recurrence problem; establish which record you are viewing first.

If the provider is correct but the app differs, report the app and iOS versions, calendar type, intended scope and dates affected. If the provider also changed more dates than intended, contact the organizer or provider support before making further broad edits. Avoid removing accounts, cancelling invitations or deleting a series as diagnostic steps.

practical: Write down which occurrence dates should change and which should stay the same.
Confirm the owning calendar and organizer or editing permission.
For a one-off exception, use an editor that explicitly offers that scope.
Check an earlier date, the changed date and the next ordinary occurrence.
Keep existing exceptions and the original invitation while diagnosing a mismatch.

faq.q: Does every recurring-event edit ask about scope?
faq.a: No. The reviewed Cloud Calendars save path does not establish that prompt. Verify the options in the editor before saving, especially for a single-date change.

faq.q: Should every recurring event have an end date?
faq.a: Use an end date when the real schedule has one. Continuing commitments do not need an invented deadline simply to make the calendar tidier.

faq.q: Will changing the series erase its exceptions?
faq.a: There is no universal answer across providers and edit operations. Record important exceptions and inspect them after the change; do not assume either guaranteed preservation or automatic loss.
